lesson.title: Stitching the Lagging Strand: Okazaki Fragments
lesson.summary: The lagging strand of DNA is built as a series of short segments called Okazaki fragments, each started with its own primer and later joined into one continuous strand by DNA ligase.
lesson.body:
In the previous chapter, we saw why the lagging strand cannot be synthesized in one continuous piece the way the leading strand can: DNA polymerase can only build in the 5' to 3' direction, and on the lagging strand template that means synthesis has to move away from the replication fork rather than following it. The short pieces of DNA produced this way are called Okazaki fragments, named after Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki, who first identified them through experiments on replicating E. coli DNA in the 1960s.

Here is how a single fragment comes together. As the replication fork opens and exposes more of the lagging strand template, primase lays down a short RNA primer close to the fork, giving DNA polymerase the free 3'-OH end it needs to begin working (recall from the DNA Polymerase chapter that DNA polymerase cannot start a strand without a primer). DNA polymerase then extends that primer, synthesizing DNA away from the fork until it runs into the primer of the previously made fragment, at which point it stops. This cycle then repeats: a new primer is laid down closer to the fork, and another fragment is synthesized, and so on, for as long as the fork continues to open.

At this stage, the lagging strand is a row of separate fragments, each still carrying a stretch of RNA primer at its 5' end and a gap where that primer needs to be replaced with DNA. A different DNA polymerase then removes each RNA primer and fills the resulting gap with the correct DNA nucleotides. Finally, an enzyme called DNA ligase seals the remaining nick, the small break in the sugar-phosphate backbone between the end of one fragment and the beginning of the next, by catalyzing the formation of the last phosphodiester bond. Only after ligase has done its work is the lagging strand truly one continuous, unbroken strand of DNA.

For example, imagine the lagging strand being built as fragment one covering the first 150 nucleotides nearest the origin, followed by fragment two covering the next 150 nucleotides closer to the fork. Fragment two's primer is laid down and extended until it reaches the RNA primer left at the start of fragment one; that primer is removed and replaced with DNA, and ligase then seals the gap between the two fragments, so the DNA reads as one uninterrupted strand rather than two spliced-together pieces.

This fragment-by-fragment, primer-dependent way of building the lagging strand is not just a technical detail. It has a direct and important consequence at the very ends of a linear chromosome, since there is no upstream fragment to extend into the gap left by the very last primer. That consequence, and how cells cope with it, is exactly the subject of the Telomeres chapter later in this unit.
